title: Drone Kits vs Curriculum: What Schools Actually Need
sub_heading: Hardware gets attention; structured Part 107 prep and teacher visibility are what make a program credibly run.
body_html:
Draft — review before import.

In short: Kits and airframes are one layer of a school drone program. FAA Part 107 knowledge test prep, assessments, and org-level progress tracking are the software layer that outlasts any single model of quadcopter.

What kits and labs provide

Hands-on stick time, team projects, maintenance habits, and excitement. Simulators and low-cost trainers reduce crash cost. Flight labs still need airspace awareness, instructor oversight, and insurance—topics the knowledge course supports.

What curriculum software provides

Structured units aligned to Part 107 ACS domains, hundreds of practice questions, unit and course exams, and a manager dashboard so teachers see who is prepared for the FAA knowledge test.

Common school mistake

Buying hardware first, then scrambling for assessable content. Reverse the order when budget is sequential: define credential outcomes, then add flight lab hours that complement—not replace—exam prep.

Questions answered

We already own drones—do we need this?

Often yes for the knowledge test and accountability layer unless you already have structured assessments and cohort tracking.

Do you sell drones?

No. Drone Edge is software; hardware is separate.
